comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral findings (C8-C10, C57-C64, C73, C131). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED with high confidence. OpenEval emphasizes methodological strengths (within-subject design, statistical power, residual velocity approach), while peer reviewers describe findings as 'solid' and provide 'clear causal evidence.' No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on EEG findings (C12-C14, C80-C85). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the paradoxical finding that THP both strengthens CNV and slows RT requires complex interpretation. Peer reviewers accept the findings but Reviewer 2 notes 'The EEG results do not shape a concrete mechanism of action,' suggesting acceptance of data but questioning mechanistic interpretation. OpenEval addresses this with dual-mechanism interpretation (C109-C111).

Divergent evaluations of exploratory whole-brain EEG analyses (C15-C17, C87-C88, C140-C144). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, citing reduced power, authors' own cautions, and need for replication. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 affirming the authors 'link these behavioral effects to motor preparatory signatures.' This represents a meaningful difference in interpretation of exploratory findings with acknowledged limitations.

Divergent evaluations of mediation analysis (C18-C19, C101-C102, C145-C153). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing proper methodology and that all Baron & Kenny criteria were met. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with concerns about small sample size (N=20) and Reviewer 2's statement that 'The EEG results do not shape a concrete mechanism of action.' Both acknowledge small effect sizes, but differ on whether this undermines confidence in the findings.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding mediated moderation analysis (C20-C21, C103, C154-C159). Both rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval cites weak significance (p=0.0132), very small effect size (Δβ=-0.0008), reduced power, and speculative interpretation. Peer reviewers echo these concerns, emphasizing small sample size and need for replication. Both evaluations converge on cautious interpretation pending further evidence.

Agreement on distractor effects (C65-C67, C70-C71, C74, C116). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes drug×distractor interaction is well-supported but interpretation of reduced repulsion as weaker attentional suppression is 'somewhat speculative.' Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly affirms the findings show 'muscarinic antagonism...modulates the distractibility of participants.' Minor difference: peer R6 includes C121-C123 not in OpenEval R6.

Both address null effect of incentives on distraction (C68). OpenEval R6 includes this as part of broader distractor analysis, noting it's 'appropriately qualified by the speed-accuracy analysis (C69).' Peer R7 treats this as separate finding, rating it SUPPORTED as a negative result with methodological explanation (C120). Agreement on acceptance of null finding but different organizational approaches.

Perfect agreement on study limitations (C124-C126). Both rate as SUPPORTED (appropriately acknowledged). OpenEval provides specific power calculations (planned N=27 for 0.8 power, achieved N=20 giving 0.7 power). Peer reviewers emphasize all three reviewers explicitly noted small sample size as weakness and limitation to males affects generalizability. Both agree limitations don't invalidate main findings but require caution with exploratory analyses.

OpenEval R7 addresses ERP component dissociations (C75-C79) showing P3a and late incentive-cue response patterns provide specificity for THP effects on action preparation versus general incentive processing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - this specific analysis of ERP component dissociations was not explicitly discussed in peer reviews.

OpenEval R8 addresses methodological justification for residual velocity approach (C134-C136), rating it as SUPPORTED with strong prior validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not specifically comment on this methodological choice, though they accepted the behavioral findings that used this measure.
